category: Formal, legal, literary, and archaic conjunctions

entries.clause: reduced concessive clause — normally a phrase, not a full clause
entries.pattern: [main clause], albeit [adjective / adverb / noun phrase / prepositional phrase]. · [article] [adjective], albeit [adjective], [noun]. · [main clause], albeit that [clause] (rare and dated).
entries.punctuation: Comma before albeit when it introduces a trailing phrase; commas on both sides when the phrase sits inside the clause. No semicolon — it is a subordinator, not a conjunctive adverb.
variants: all be it (the original three-word form, no longer written)
entries.meaning: A formal concessive meaning although it be. Its one distinguishing habit is that, unlike although, it almost never takes a full finite clause in modern American English — it heads a bare phrase (albeit reluctantly, albeit a costly one), which is exactly why it is so convenient in edited prose. Writing albeit he was tired is not wrong historically but reads as a mistake today.
examples: The plan worked, albeit more slowly than we had hoped.
She agreed to help, albeit reluctantly.
It was a victory, albeit a costly one.
The restaurant serves very good food, albeit at prices that make you wince.
He is a talented, albeit difficult, collaborator.
The policy has been revised, albeit only in the margins.

entries.clause: sentence adverbial of concession — modifies the whole following clause
entries.pattern: [clause]. Be that as it may, [clause]. · [clause]; be that as it may, [clause].
entries.punctuation: Takes a semicolon or a period before it and a comma after it. A comma alone before it produces a comma splice — this is a sentence adverb, not a conjunction.
entries.meaning: A frozen subjunctive clause — literally let that be as it may be — used to concede the previous point and then set it aside. It differs from however in what it concedes: however signals mere contrast, while be that as it may grants that the other side may well be right and says the conclusion stands anyway.
examples: The budget is tight. Be that as it may, the roof still has to be replaced.
He may have meant no harm; be that as it may, the damage is done.
Be that as it may, I would like to hear the other side before I decide.
She apologized, and the apology seemed sincere. Be that as it may, the policy requires a written report.
The data is three years old. Be that as it may, it is the only data we have.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of concessive condition ("no matter how")
entries.pattern: Howsoever [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · Howsoever [adjective/adverb] [subject] (may be), [main clause]. · [main clause] howsoever [subject] [verb]. · [noun/participle] howsoever [prepositional phrase] (legal boilerplate, no commas).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the howsoever clause when it comes first; no comma when it follows. Inside a noun phrase in legal boilerplate (any claim arising howsoever out of this Agreement) it takes no punctuation at all. Never a semicolon — the semicolon rule belongs to the conjunctive adverb however, not to this word.
entries.meaning: The emphatic -soever form of however in its subordinating sense: no matter how, in whatever way. Its whole family — whosoever, wheresoever, whensoever, whatsoever — is built the same way and survives in legal boilerplate (any claim whatsoever) and in scripture. Do not confuse it with the conjunctive adverb however (= nevertheless), which needs a semicolon; howsoever never does.
examples: Howsoever the vote goes, we will respect the outcome.
The trustee may invest the funds howsoever he sees fit.
Howsoever slight the risk, it must be disclosed to the patient.
Any claim arising howsoever out of this Agreement shall be settled by arbitration.
Howsoever she explained it, the committee remained unconvinced.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession (= although … very much)
entries.pattern: Much as [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · [main clause], much as [subject] [verb]. · As much as [subject] [verb], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted much as clause — and it is fronted the great majority of the time. Comma before a trailing much as clause as well, because it always comments on the whole main clause rather than restricting it. Never a semicolon: it is a subordinator, not a conjunctive adverb.
variants: as much as (the same conjunction with the fuller opening)
entries.meaning: A concessive that concedes an intensity: Much as I admire her, I cannot vote for her means "although I admire her a great deal." Because the degree word is doing the concessive work, the verb has to be one that admits of degree — admire, want, like, regret, tempt. Keep it apart from the comparative as much as meaning "the same quantity as" (He earns as much as I do): the concessive fronts its clause and takes a comma, the comparative does neither.
examples: Much as I admire her work, I cannot vote for her.
Much as he wanted the job, he turned it down once he read the contract.
She refused to sell the house, much as the offer tempted her.
Much as it pains me to admit it, the first draft was the better one.
As much as we would like to help, the fund is already committed for the year.
Much as the team improved after the trade, it still finished last in the division.

entries.type: subordinating (with that); preposition and postposition elsewhere
entries.clause: adverbial clause of concession with that; otherwise a concessive prepositional phrase
entries.pattern: Notwithstanding [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [noun phrase] notwithstanding, [main clause]. · Notwithstanding that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] notwithstanding [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase in all three fronted patterns, including the postposed one (Her objections notwithstanding, the board approved it). No comma when a plain notwithstanding + noun phrase trails the main clause (The contract remains in force notwithstanding any change of ownership) — but a comma is required when the postposed form trails, since that is an absolute construction (He signed the lease, his lawyer's warnings notwithstanding). Never a semicolon: it introduces a phrase or a subordinate clause, not a second independent clause.
entries.meaning: The heavyweight concessive of American legal drafting, where notwithstanding anything to the contrary herein is the standard way to make one clause override another. Its distinguishing trick — unique among English concessives — is that it can follow its own object (the delay notwithstanding), a leftover word order no other preposition allows.
examples: Notwithstanding the weather, the ceremony went ahead outdoors.
The contract remains in force notwithstanding any change of ownership.
Her objections notwithstanding, the board approved the merger.
Notwithstanding that the deadline had passed, the court accepted the filing.
Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in Section 4, the Buyer shall pay all closing costs.
He signed the lease, his lawyer's warnings notwithstanding.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (simultaneity) or of contrast
entries.pattern: Whilst [subject] [verb], [main clause]. · [main clause] whilst [subject] [verb] (simultaneity). · [main clause], whilst [subject] [verb] (contrast). · [main clause] whilst [-ing phrase / reduced clause].
entries.punctuation: Identical to while: comma after the whilst clause when it comes first; no comma before a trailing clause of simultaneity (She studied Latin whilst she was at Cambridge), but a comma before a trailing clause that draws a contrast (The museum is open daily, whilst the archive opens only by appointment).
entries.meaning: A British variant of while with no difference in meaning — it covers both simultaneity and contrast exactly as while does. It is listed here because American learners meet it constantly in British books, journals, and corporate boilerplate and reasonably conclude it is the more formal English word. It is not: an American editor will change every instance to while, and using it in American prose reads as affectation. Its cousins amongst and amidst are prepositions rather than conjunctions, but carry the same British flavor and get the same treatment from an American editor. One limit worth knowing: only the conjunction has an -st form. While is also a noun (stay a while, worth your while) and a verb (while away an afternoon), and neither of those is ever whilst, in Britain or anywhere else.
examples: Whilst the report is thorough, it stops short of a recommendation. (British usage)
She studied Latin whilst she was at Cambridge. (British usage)
Passengers are asked to remain seated whilst the aircraft is taxiing. (British usage)
Whilst I appreciate the offer, I must decline. (British usage)
He read the paper whilst his tea went cold. (British usage)
The museum is open daily, whilst the archive opens only by appointment. (British usage)

entries.clause: adverbial clause of cause
entries.pattern: Forasmuch as [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], forasmuch as [clause] (rare).
entries.punctuation: Comma after the forasmuch as clause when it is fronted, which is nearly always. A trailing forasmuch as clause is possible but rare even in period prose, and it takes a comma before it, because it comments on the whole main clause rather than restricting it. Never a semicolon.
entries.meaning: A causal conjunction meaning seeing that, since. Where inasmuch as narrowed to "to the extent that" and stayed alive, forasmuch as stayed purely causal and died everywhere except the Book of Common Prayer, the King James Bible, and the preambles of old statutes and judgments. An American meets it at funerals and in nineteenth-century legal reports.
examples: Forasmuch as it hath pleased Almighty God to take unto himself the soul of our departed brother, we commit his body to the ground. (after the Book of Common Prayer)
Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us … (King James Bible)
Forasmuch as the parties have agreed to settle all claims between them, this action is dismissed with prejudice.
Forasmuch as the defendant has admitted liability, the trial will address damages only.
Forasmuch as no objection was filed within the statutory period, the plan is hereby confirmed.
The award will not be disturbed, forasmuch as no fraud has been shown. (the rarer trailing order)

entries.clause: adverbial clause of cause or respect
entries.pattern: [main clause] in that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Normally no comma before in that — it restricts the main clause rather than commenting on it. It cannot be fronted: In that it assumes constant demand, the argument is flawed is not idiomatic. Never a semicolon.
variants: insofar as (when the point is scope rather than respect)
entries.meaning: A formal causal conjunction that specifies the respect in which the main clause is true, rather than the reason it happened. Do not read it as the preposition in plus the demonstrative that (the receipts are in that folder): the conjunction is a fixed two-word unit and is always followed by a complete clause, never by a noun. Contrast because: The argument is flawed because it assumes constant demand says the assumption caused the flaw; The argument is flawed in that it assumes constant demand says the assumption is the flaw. It is the standard connective of academic and judicial prose for exactly that reason, and it is the only entry in this section a modern American would write unselfconsciously.
examples: The argument is flawed in that it assumes the very thing it sets out to prove.
This case is unusual in that both parties agree on every material fact.
She was fortunate in that her injuries turned out to be minor.
The new statute differs from the old one in that it applies to contractors as well as employees.
The study is limited in that it draws on a single hospital system.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of cause, or of degree/respect
entries.pattern: Inasmuch as [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] inasmuch as [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the inasmuch as clause when it is fronted; normally no comma when it follows. Never a semicolon.
variants: insomuch as (a different word — see below)
entries.meaning: Two related senses: because (Inasmuch as the plaintiff failed to appear, the case is dismissed) and to the extent that (He is responsible inasmuch as he approved the transfer). The second is the live one in modern legal and academic writing. Keep it apart from insomuch as, which means to such a degree that and introduces a result rather than a cause — the two are confused constantly, and the -a- versus -o- is the only signal.
examples: The ruling is significant inasmuch as it overturns forty years of precedent.
Inasmuch as the plaintiff failed to appear, the case is dismissed for want of prosecution.
He is responsible inasmuch as he approved the transfer without reading it.
Inasmuch as we are all volunteers here, nobody is going to be fired over a missed meeting.
The two cases are alike inasmuch as both turn on the meaning of the word "reasonable."
Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me. (King James Bible)

entries.clause: adverbial clause of result or degree
entries.pattern: [main clause], insomuch that [clause]. · [main clause] insomuch as [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma before insomuch that when it introduces a consequence, because the result comments on the whole main clause rather than restricting it. No comma before the degree sense insomuch as, which does restrict the main clause (He was trusted insomuch as he was given a key). It is not fronted, and it never takes a semicolon: what follows is a subordinate clause, not a second independent one.
entries.meaning: Means to such a degree that — it introduces the result of what the main clause described (The wind rose, insomuch that the ferry was canceled). Its near-twin inasmuch as introduces a cause. A useful test: insomuch looks forward to a consequence and can usually be replaced by so … that; inasmuch looks backward to a reason and can be replaced by since.
examples: The wind rose through the afternoon, insomuch that the last ferry was canceled.
The evidence was overwhelming, insomuch that the defense rested without calling a single witness.
The crowd pressed forward, insomuch that the officers had to link arms.
He was trusted insomuch as he was given a key to the building.
The drought ran three straight years, insomuch that the riverbed cracked open.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of negative purpose, or complement of an expression of fear
entries.pattern: [main clause] lest [subject] [bare verb]. · [main clause] lest [subject] should [verb]. · Lest [subject] [bare verb], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before lest when it follows the main clause and states a purpose; a comma is used when it comments on the whole preceding clause (The committee moved quickly, lest the opportunity be lost). Comma after a fronted lest clause. Never a semicolon — lest subordinates a clause, it does not join two independent ones.
entries.meaning: Introduces the outcome to be avoided, so it is inherently negative: lest already contains the not, and writing lest he should not forget reverses your meaning. Two things mark it as formal. It takes the bare subjunctive — lest he forget, never lest he forgets — and it is one of the last places in American English where that mood is obligatory rather than optional.
examples: He wrote the address on the back of his hand lest he forget it.
The committee moved quickly, lest the opportunity be lost.
She kept her voice down lest the neighbors hear.
Lest anyone think this is a minor matter, the fine is fifty thousand dollars.
I am putting it in writing lest there be any confusion later.
He hesitated to ask, lest she should take offense.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of purpose
entries.pattern: [main clause] to the end that [subject] may/might/shall/should [verb]. · [main clause], to the end that [clause]. · To the end that [subject] may/might/shall/should [verb], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: When it trails, a comma before it is optional and signals that the purpose comments on the whole main clause rather than restricting it. When it is fronted — much rarer, and confined to drafting — a comma closes the to the end that clause. Never a semicolon.
variants: in order that (the neutral formal equivalent)
entries.meaning: The ceremonial purpose conjunction: so that, dressed for court. It strongly prefers a modal in its clause — may, might, shall, or should — and sounds wrong with a bare present tense. The bare literary that of Speak, that I may hear thee is the same construction with the noun phrase worn away.
examples: The records are sealed to the end that witnesses may testify without fear of reprisal.
Notice shall be published once a week for three weeks, to the end that all creditors may present their claims.
He left the whole of his estate to the college, to the end that no student should be turned away for want of money.
The rules were tightened to the end that such an accident might never happen again.
We publish these findings to the end that others may build on them.
To the end that the record may be complete, the clerk shall file all correspondence received in the matter.

entries.type: quasi-coordinator — exceptive; prepositional before a noun phrase
entries.clause: exceptive phrase; before a bare infinitive it introduces a reduced clause
entries.pattern: [no one / none / nothing / nobody / all / who] but [noun phrase]. · [nothing / no choice / no option] but [bare infinitive].
entries.punctuation: No comma. The exceptive but binds tightly to what follows it and is never punctuated like the coordinating but, which does take a comma before it when it joins two independent clauses.
entries.meaning: This is not the FANBOYS but — it means except, and it survives in fixed negative frames: none but, nothing but, no one but, all but, no choice but. Before a bare infinitive it is a genuine subordinator (nothing to do but wait). One old refinement is still argued over: because it was historically a conjunction, formal usage takes the nominative after it (no one but he knew), while ordinary American English treats it as a preposition and says no one but him. Few English words spread across more classes: but is a coordinating conjunction (small but sturdy), this exceptive preposition, a degree adverb meaning only (he is but a child, there were but three left), a counterfactual in the compound but for, and even a noun (no ifs, ands, or buts). Only the coordinating one takes a comma before it when it joins two independent clauses.
examples: None but the brave deserves the fair. (Dryden)
There was nothing to do but wait for the tow truck.
No one but a fool would sign a lease like that.
All but two of the seats were already taken.
He had no choice but to resign.
Who but a native speaker would ever catch that?

entries.type: quasi-coordinator — counterfactual prepositional connective; not a clause introducer
entries.clause: counterfactual conditional phrase; the main clause carries would or would have
entries.pattern: But for [noun phrase], [main clause with would / would have]. · [main clause with would / would have] but for [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted but for phrase; no comma when it trails the main clause. Never a semicolon — it introduces a phrase, not a second independent clause. Hyphenated when it is pressed into service as a modifier: but-for causation, the but-for world.
variants: absent (the drafting equivalent: absent the storm)
entries.meaning: The counterfactual but: it names the one circumstance whose absence would have changed the outcome, so the main clause is contrary to fact and nearly always carries would or would have. It is a fixture of American tort law, where but-for causation is the basic test — an act is a cause of the harm if the harm would not have happened but for it. Keep it apart from the exceptive but directly above: exceptive but subtracts a member from a set (no one but the pilot), while but for subtracts a condition from a history.
examples: But for the storm, the ceremony would have been held outdoors.
She would have made partner years ago but for the merger.
But for a single misplaced decimal, the audit would have passed without comment.
The plaintiff must show that the injury would not have occurred but for the defendant's negligence.
But for his testimony, there would have been no case at all.
The building would still be standing but for a faulty relay in the alarm panel.

entries.clause: noun clause after a negated expression of doubt; or adverbial clause of exception
entries.pattern: [negated doubt/denial] but that [clause]. · But that [clause], [main clause]. · [not so ADJ] but that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted but that clause. No comma after a verb of doubting or denying, where the clause is the verb's own object (I do not doubt but that …), and none after not so + adjective. A comma before a trailing but that clause when it means were it not that (She would have left years ago, but that her mother needed looking after). Never a semicolon.
entries.meaning: Three formal uses. After a negated verb of doubting or denying it simply fills in for that (There is no question but that the statute applies). Fronted, it means were it not that (But that I trusted him, I would never have handed over the keys) and takes past-tense or subjunctive forms. And after not so …, it means that … not (no case so hopeless but that something can be salvaged).
examples: I do not doubt but that the money will be repaid in full.
There is no question but that the statute applies to these facts.
But that I trusted him completely, I would never have handed over the keys.
She would have left years ago, but that her mother needed looking after.
No case is so hopeless but that something can be salvaged from it.

entries.clause: reduced adverbial clause of exception; the as clause stands in for whatever the other provision says
entries.pattern: Except as otherwise provided [in Section X / herein], [main clause]. · Unless otherwise provided [in X], [main clause]. · [main clause] except as otherwise provided in [X].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted formula, which is where drafters deliberately put it so that the reader meets the carve-out before the rule. No comma when it trails the main clause. Never a semicolon — what follows the formula is the main clause itself, not a second independent one.
variants: except as otherwise set forth herein
entries.meaning: The standard American drafting formula for making one provision yield to another, and the mirror image of notwithstanding: except as otherwise provided in Section 9 means Section 9 wins, while notwithstanding Section 9 means this clause wins. Unless otherwise provided is the same formula with a conditional opener instead of an exceptive one and is used interchangeably. The danger both carry is vagueness — a bare except as otherwise provided herein points at the whole document at once, which is why careful drafters name the section.
examples: Except as otherwise provided in this Article, all notices required by this Agreement must be given in writing.
Unless otherwise provided by law, the annual meeting shall be held at the principal office of the corporation.
Except as otherwise provided herein, each party bears its own costs and attorneys' fees.
The Tenant shall pay all utilities furnished to the premises, except as otherwise provided in Section 6.3.
Unless otherwise provided in the applicable purchase order, delivery terms are FOB destination.
Except as otherwise provided in subsection (b), an application must be filed within ninety days of the denial.

entries.register: neutral to formal (bare except is informal)
entries.clause: adverbial clause of exception
entries.pattern: [main clause], except that [clause]. · [main clause] except that [clause]. · Except that [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: A comma before except that is usual when the exception qualifies the whole main clause, and omitted when it attaches to a single element. Comma after a fronted except that clause. Never a semicolon.
entries.meaning: The everyday exceptive conjunction and the modern replacement for save that. It subtracts one detail from a claim that is otherwise true. Dropping that is fully idiomatic in speech (I would have called, except my phone was dead), but the two-word form is what edited prose uses. Note that this is a different word from the archaic except meaning unless. Except runs across three classes in all: preposition (everyone except me), conjunction (this entry and the archaic unless sense), and verb (present company excepted) — and only the clause-taking uses are punctuated as above.
examples: The apartment is close to perfect, except that the radiator clanks all night.
Nothing about the place had changed, except that the sign over the door was new.
I would have called you, except that my phone was dead.
The two drafts are identical except that the second adds a severability clause.
He remembers nothing at all about the accident, except that it was raining.
Except that it rained hard on Saturday, the trip went exactly as planned.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition (a proviso limiting the clause before it)
entries.pattern: [main clause]; provided always that [clause]. · [main clause]; provided, however, that [clause]. · [main clause], provided that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Both marks are in use, and they mean different things. A semicolon is the drafting convention when the proviso cuts back the entire preceding provision, and it is effectively obligatory before provided, however, that; a comma is normal when the proviso attaches to the immediately preceding clause only, and it is what ordinary formal prose uses with plain provided that. In the provided, however, that form, both commas around however are required — dropping them is one of the most visible tells of sloppy drafting. Note that the semicolon here does not make this a conjunctive adverb: what follows is a subordinate clause, not an independent one.
entries.meaning: The contract proviso: a condition attached after the fact to cut back the grant just made. The plain conditional provided that is ordinary formal English and belongs with the everyday conditionals; provided always that and provided, however, that are drafting formulas whose job is to signal that an exception to the foregoing is coming. Careful drafters now prefer except that or a separate sentence, because a proviso's scope — how far back it reaches — is a classic source of litigation.
examples: The Tenant may sublet the premises; provided always that the Landlord's written consent is first obtained.
Payment shall be made within thirty days, provided always that a conforming invoice has been received.
The license granted herein is perpetual; provided, however, that it terminates immediately upon a breach of Section 7.
The Trustee may sell any asset of the trust, provided always that the sale is at fair market value.
Employees may work remotely, provided always that their supervisor approves the arrangement in advance.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition — a second proviso stacked on the first
entries.pattern: [main clause]; provided that [clause]; provided further that [clause]. · [main clause]; provided further, however, that [clause].
entries.punctuation: A semicolon before it, effectively always: by the time a second proviso arrives the sentence has at least three parts, and the semicolon is what keeps them apart. Further takes no commas around it, unlike the however of provided, however, that. The semicolon here is a drafting convention rather than the conjunctive-adverb rule — what follows is a subordinate clause, not an independent one.
entries.meaning: The marker of a stacked proviso: it adds a second condition to the one just stated rather than cutting it back. That is the whole difference from provided, however, that, which is adversative. Strings of these — provided that … provided further that … provided further that — are the signature of nineteenth-century American statutes and appropriations bills, and are exactly why modern drafting manuals tell you to break the sentence apart and number the conditions instead.
examples: The Secretary may extend the deadline; provided that the applicant has shown good cause; provided further that no extension shall exceed ninety days.
The Tenant may sublet the premises; provided that the Landlord consents in writing; provided further that the subtenant assumes every obligation of this Lease.
The sum appropriated shall remain available until expended; provided further that not more than ten percent may be used for administration.
Payment shall be made within thirty days of invoice; provided further that interest accrues on any unpaid balance from the date of the invoice.
The permit may be renewed annually; provided further, however, that renewal shall be refused while any fee remains unpaid.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition — an adversative proviso cutting back what precedes
entries.pattern: [main clause]; provided, however, that [clause]. · [main clause]; provided, however, that [clause]; and provided further that [clause].
entries.punctuation: A semicolon before it and commas on both sides of however. Both commas are required, and dropping either is the most visible tell of careless drafting. The semicolon does not make this a conjunctive adverb: however is buried inside a subordinator here, and what follows is a subordinate clause. A comma in place of the semicolon is not a comma splice, but it blurs how far back the proviso reaches — the single most litigated question about provisos.
entries.meaning: The adversative proviso: however announces that the condition about to be stated takes something back from the grant just made. Against provided further that, which adds a second condition, this one contradicts the first; against plain provided that, which is ordinary formal English, this one is pure drafting formula. American style authorities — Garner most insistently — advise replacing the whole thing with but or except that, or with a separate sentence.
examples: The license granted herein is perpetual; provided, however, that it terminates immediately upon a breach of Section 7.
Either party may terminate on thirty days' written notice; provided, however, that termination shall not affect obligations already accrued.
The Company shall reimburse all reasonable travel expenses; provided, however, that any expense over one thousand dollars requires prior written approval.
The Buyer may inspect the goods at any reasonable time; provided, however, that no inspection shall delay shipment.
This Agreement is governed by the law of Delaware; provided, however, that the arbitration clause is governed by the Federal Arbitration Act.

entries.type: quasi-coordinator — exceptive; prepositional before a noun phrase
entries.clause: exceptive phrase subtracted from the main clause
entries.pattern: [all / every / none / nothing / no one] [predicate] save [noun phrase]. · [main clause] save for [noun phrase]. · [main clause], save for [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: No comma when save attaches directly to the exhaustive word it subtracts from (all the passengers save the pilot). A comma when the exception trails the whole clause as an afterthought, which is the usual pattern with save for (The room was empty, save for a folding chair). Never a semicolon — it introduces a phrase, not a second independent clause.
entries.meaning: The literary except. It sits between the exhaustive word (all, every, none, nothing) and the one item pulled out of it. Save for is the commoner modern form and is the one you will actually meet in journalism and fiction. Do not confuse it with the verb save: He saved one and all save one look alike and are unrelated. Four word classes share the spelling — verb (save the file), noun (the goalie's save), this exceptive preposition, and, with that added, a full subordinating conjunction — and only the last of those takes a clause.
examples: Every window on the street was dark save one.
The room was empty, save for a folding chair and a coffee can full of nails.
All the passengers save the pilot survived the landing.
Nothing remained of the barn save the foundation.
He told no one save his wife.

entries.clause: exceptive phrase carving one thing out of a larger grant; with that, an adverbial clause of exception
entries.pattern: [grant of the whole] save and except [noun phrase]. · [grant], save and except that [clause]. · SAVE AND EXCEPTING therefrom [description of the parcel reserved].
entries.punctuation: No comma when it attaches directly to the thing it subtracts from, which is the ordinary case in a deed. A comma when the exception trails the whole clause as an afterthought. Never a semicolon — it introduces a phrase, or with that a subordinate clause, and neither is a second independent clause.
entries.meaning: A legal doublet: save is the native English exceptive and except the Latin-derived one, welded together by the old drafting habit of pairing an English word with its Romance twin — the same instinct behind will and testament and free and clear. It survives in American deeds and mineral conveyances, where a save and except clause is how a seller keeps back a strip, a road, or the mineral rights while conveying everything else. Plain-drafting guides would have you write except; title examiners will be reading the doublet for as long as there are deeds.
examples: The Grantor conveys all of Lot 14, save and except the westerly twenty feet reserved for the county road.
All of the Grantor's interest in the land described above is conveyed, save and except all oil, gas, and other minerals, which are reserved unto the Grantor.
The sale includes every fixture in the building, save and except the walk-in cooler.
SAVE AND EXCEPTING therefrom that portion heretofore conveyed to the school district by deed recorded in Book 212, Page 40.
The release covers claims of every kind, save and except that it does not extend to claims for indemnity under Section 9.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of exception
entries.pattern: [main clause], save that [clause]. · Save that [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma before save that when it trails the main clause, and after the clause when it is fronted. Never a semicolon — what follows is a subordinate clause, not an independent one.
entries.meaning: The clause-taking counterpart of save, and a straight formal substitute for except that. It is the standard way in contract drafting to carve one exception out of a provision you have just stated, and in literary prose it introduces the one detail that survives an otherwise blank memory (He remembered nothing, save that it had ended badly).
examples: The two texts are identical, save that the later one drops a footnote.
He remembered nothing of the evening, save that it had ended badly.
The terms are unchanged, save that the annual fee increases by three percent.
Save that she signed the register, there is no evidence she was ever in the building.
Nothing in this Section limits the Buyer's remedies, save that consequential damages are excluded.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of proportion or correspondence
entries.pattern: [main clause] according as [clause]. · According as [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma when it follows the main clause; comma after a fronted according as clause. Never a semicolon.
entries.meaning: Sets up a correspondence: the main clause varies in step with the subordinate one. Modern English says according to whether or simply depending on whether, which is why according as now appears only in older statutes, actuarial and tax language, and nineteenth-century prose. Note that according to takes a noun phrase and according as takes a clause — that is the whole difference.
examples: The tax is calculated according as the property is residential or commercial.
Members will be seated according as they arrive.
The grant is renewed or withdrawn according as the trustees judge the work to be sound.
He praised or blamed the crew according as the day had gone well or badly.
The payment rises or falls according as the index rises or falls.
According as the harvest was good or poor, the rent was raised or forgiven.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of degree or extent
entries.pattern: [main clause] insofar as [clause]. · Insofar as [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma when it follows the main clause; comma after a fronted insofar as clause. Never a semicolon.
variants: to the extent that (the plainer equivalent)
entries.meaning: Limits a claim to the degree it actually holds: The rule applies insofar as it does not conflict with federal law concedes that beyond that point it does not apply. Americans write it closed up as one word; the British write in so far as. Against inasmuch as, which is chiefly causal, insofar as is chiefly about scope, and to the extent that is the plain-English substitute a modern drafting guide will push you toward.
examples: The state rule applies insofar as it does not conflict with federal law.
Insofar as I can tell, the two accounts agree on every material point.
He was helpful insofar as he handed over the file, but he would not explain any of it.
The company is liable insofar as its employees were acting within the scope of their duties.
Insofar as the treaty covers fishing rights, it remains in force.

entries.clause: relative clause of place/source, or interrogative noun clause
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] whence [clause]. · [verb of knowing/saying] whence [clause]. · Whence [verb] [subject]? · [main clause], whence [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma before whence when it comments on the whole preceding clause (a crawlspace, whence a raccoon emerged); no comma when it restricts a noun, and none before an indirect question (no one could say whence the rumor had started). Never a semicolon.
variants: from whence (long established, though strictly redundant)
entries.meaning: Means from where or from which — the from is already inside the word. That makes from whence a redundancy, which purists have objected to for three centuries and which the King James Bible uses anyway (from whence cometh my help), so it is best called long-established rather than wrong. It completes a set with whither (to where) and where (at where).
examples: They went back to the village whence they had come.
No one could say whence the rumor had started.
The envelope gave no clue whence it had been mailed.
She traced the noise to a crawlspace, whence a very large raccoon eventually emerged.
Whence comes this sudden generosity?
I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. (King James Bible)

entries.register: archaic, formal — alive in legal boilerplate
entries.clause: adverbial clause of indefinite time ("at whatever time", "no matter when")
entries.pattern: Whensoever [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] whensoever [clause]. · [noun phrase] whensoever [participle / prepositional phrase] (boilerplate, no commas).
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted whensoever clause; no comma when it follows the main clause. Inside a noun phrase in boilerplate (any claim whensoever arising) it takes no punctuation at all. Never a semicolon — it is a subordinator, not a conjunctive adverb.
entries.meaning: The -soever form of whenever: at whatever time. Like the rest of its family it survives in exactly two places — the King James Bible and the belt-and-suspenders language of contracts and releases, where whensoever arising is written to keep any argument about timing from getting started. In ordinary American English whenever covers every use, and whensoever in modern prose reads as costume.
examples: Whensoever the Board determines that a vacancy exists, it may appoint a successor to serve out the unexpired term.
The Indemnitor shall pay all losses, whensoever arising, out of the use or operation of the equipment.
For ye have the poor with you always, and whensoever ye will ye may do them good. (King James Bible)
Any claim under this Agreement, whensoever and howsoever arising, shall be submitted to arbitration.
Whensoever the King's peace was broken, the sheriff of the county was answerable for it.

entries.clause: recital clause — a stacked background statement, not joined to a main clause
entries.pattern: WHEREAS, [clause]; · WHEREAS, [clause]; NOW, THEREFORE, [operative clause]. · Whereas [clause], [resolving clause].
entries.punctuation: In recitals each WHEREAS clause ends with a semicolon, not a comma, because the recitals are a stacked list rather than subordinate clauses attached to a main clause; the last one runs into NOW, THEREFORE. The word is conventionally capitalized and often followed by a comma. In the resolving use, where the clause does reach a main clause (Whereas the Tenant has failed to pay rent, the Landlord hereby terminates the lease), it is punctuated like any fronted subordinate clause: a comma closes it. The everyday contrastive whereas — a different word, filed with the concessives — takes a comma before a trailing clause: I like tea, whereas he likes coffee.
variants: given that, considering that (the plain equivalents)
entries.meaning: Two different words share this spelling. The everyday one is the contrastive subordinator (I like tea, whereas he likes coffee), which belongs with the other concessives. This entry is the legal recital whereas, meaning roughly given that — the word that opens each background paragraph of a contract, resolution, or preamble. Its syntax is unique: the clause never gets a main clause of its own, and the whole stack is discharged by NOW, THEREFORE.
examples: WHEREAS, the Company desires to retain the Consultant's services;
WHEREAS, the Consultant is willing to provide such services on the terms set forth herein;
WHEREAS the parties entered into a Master Services Agreement dated March 3, 2021, and WHEREAS the parties now wish to amend that Agreement;
Whereas it has pleased the Assembly to honor our late colleague, be it resolved that this chamber stand adjourned for the day.
Whereas the Tenant has failed to pay rent for three consecutive months, the Landlord hereby terminates the lease.

entries.clause: sentence-relative clause of reaction or point in time
entries.pattern: [clause], whereat [clause].
entries.punctuation: Always a comma before it. Like all the where- relatives it points back at the clause before it, so it cannot open a sentence.
entries.meaning: Means at which — most often at which point, introducing somebody's reaction to what has just happened. It is the rarest of the surviving where- compounds and is functionally interchangeable with whereupon, except that whereat leans toward a reaction and whereupon toward a next event.
examples: He called her a liar, whereat she picked up her coat and walked out.
The judge asked twice for silence, whereat the courtroom finally stilled.
She read the telegram, whereat all the color left her face.
The vote was announced, whereat a cheer went up from the gallery.
He proposed a toast to the bride, whereat the whole table rose.

entries.clause: relative clause modifying a noun of mechanism (system, process, arrangement)
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] whereby [clause]. · [noun phrase], whereby [clause] (nonrestrictive, rarer).
entries.punctuation: Normally no comma — it restricts the noun it follows, and a comma there is usually an error. The exception is the nonrestrictive use, where the noun is already fully identified and whereby merely adds information about it (the 1994 accord, whereby each side gave up its claims); that one takes a comma. Never a semicolon.
entries.meaning: Means by which or by means of which, and it is by a wide margin the healthiest of the where- compounds: American lawyers, journalists, and policy writers use it daily. It needs a noun of mechanism in front of it — a system, scheme, process, arrangement, mechanism, deal — and sounds wrong attached to anything else.
examples: The company has a system whereby employees can report problems anonymously.
The two sides reached an arrangement whereby each dropped its claims against the other.
The statute creates a process whereby records can be sealed after ten years.
There is no mechanism whereby a sitting member can be expelled.
He described a scheme whereby early investors would be paid out of new deposits.
The 1994 accord, whereby each side gave up its claims to the border strip, has held ever since. (nonrestrictive — hence the commas)

entries.clause: sentence adverbial of consequence; or interrogative noun clause of reason
entries.pattern: [clause]; wherefore, [clause]. · [clause]. Wherefore, [clause]. · WHEREFORE, [petitioner] prays [clause]. · Wherefore [verb] [subject]?
entries.punctuation: As a consequence marker it behaves like therefore: semicolon or period before, comma after. A comma alone before it makes a comma splice.
variants: the whys and wherefores (fixed noun phrase)
entries.meaning: Means for what reason (the archaic question word) or for which reason (the legal consequence marker). Its famous line is routinely misread: Wherefore art thou Romeo? asks why Romeo has to be a Montague, not where he is standing. In American litigation it survives as the fixed opener of the prayer for relief, WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests …, which is the last paragraph of nearly every complaint filed in the country.
examples: Wherefore art thou Romeo? (Shakespeare — "why are you Romeo," not "where are you")
WHEREFORE, Plaintiff respectfully requests that this Court enter judgment in her favor and award costs.
The defendant has failed to answer within the time allowed; wherefore, default is hereby entered.
Wherefore dost thou weep, when the thing is already done?
The board found no misconduct; wherefore, the complaint is dismissed.

entries.clause: relative clause of place or respect; or interrogative noun clause
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] wherein [clause]. · [main clause] wherein [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma when it restricts a noun; a comma when it comments on the whole preceding clause.
entries.meaning: Means in which — either literally inside something (a contract wherein the seller disclaims all warranties) or, more often, in what respect (He could not see wherein he had gone wrong). It is the second-healthiest of the where- compounds after whereby, and it is standard in judicial opinions.
examples: This is a case wherein the facts matter a great deal more than the law.
The contract contains a clause wherein the seller disclaims all warranties.
He could not see wherein he had gone wrong.
She described in detail the manner wherein the funds had been transferred.
The report identifies three areas wherein the agency exceeded its statutory authority.
She signed without reading the addendum, wherein the arbitration clause was buried. (comment on the whole clause — hence the comma)

entries.clause: relative clause of entry or destination (into which)
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] whereinto [clause]. · [noun phrase], whereinto [clause] (nonrestrictive). · [noun phrase] whereinto to [verb] (rare).
entries.punctuation: No comma when it restricts the noun it follows, which is the ordinary case; a comma in the nonrestrictive use, where the noun is already identified. Like every where- relative it points back at a noun already on the page, so it cannot open a sentence. Never a semicolon.
entries.meaning: Means into which — the motion counterpart of wherein, which is static: the room wherein he sat against the room whereinto he was led. It draws exactly the line that in and into draw in ordinary English, and it is worth noticing because wherein is often written where whereinto is meant. Outside scripture, deeds, and period narrative it is dead; into which is the living phrase.
examples: There was a garden, whereinto he entered, and his disciples. (King James Bible)
The deed describes an open cellar whereinto the surface water has drained for sixty years.
He led her down to a low chamber whereinto no daylight ever came.
This is the pit whereinto every argument of the kind eventually falls.
They came at last to a cleft in the rock, whereinto the whole company was obliged to creep one at a time.

entries.clause: relative clause modifying a noun (of which, of whom)
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] whereof [clause]. · IN WITNESS WHEREOF, [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma inside the fixed attestation formula — nothing separates WITNESS from WHEREOF — though a comma does close the formula before the main clause (IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the parties have executed …). Elsewhere, no comma when it restricts a noun. Never a semicolon.
entries.meaning: Means of which or of whom. Nearly all of its modern life is inside one frozen formula — IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the signature line that closes almost every American contract, where it means in witness of which. Outside that formula it is purely literary.
examples: IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the parties have executed this Agreement as of the date first written above.
He spoke at length of matters whereof he had no direct knowledge.
Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent. (Wittgenstein, in translation)
The document bears the seal whereof mention is made in Section 2.
She testified to events whereof she was the only living witness.

entries.clause: relative clause of location or basis (on which)
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] whereon [clause]. · [noun phrase] whereon to [verb]. · [noun phrase], whereon [clause] (nonrestrictive).
entries.punctuation: No comma when it restricts the noun it follows, which is the ordinary case. A comma only in the nonrestrictive use, where the noun is already identified (the north field, whereon the barn once stood). Never a semicolon, and it cannot open a sentence — like every where- relative it points back at a noun already on the page.
entries.meaning: Means on which, both physically (the rock whereon the church is built) and abstractly (the ground whereon the claim rests). It is the locative half of a word that split in two: whereupon took over the time sense — immediately after which — and left whereon with the literal on, which is why whereon now sounds the older of the twins although the two were once interchangeable. In American prose it survives in deeds, land descriptions, and scriptural echo, and it takes a to-infinitive as readily as wherewith does.
examples: This is the rock whereon the whole argument is built.
The deed describes the parcel whereon the mill formerly stood.
He pointed to the chair whereon the coat had been left.
She had no ground whereon to base an appeal.
The north field, whereon the barn once stood, has been planted in corn for forty years.
Every claim whereon the plaintiff relies was pleaded in the original complaint.

entries.clause: relative clause of destination or purpose (to which); or interrogative noun clause (to what end)
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] whereto [clause]. · [noun phrase] whereto [subject] [is/are + past participle]. · Whereto [verb] [subject]? (interrogative).
entries.punctuation: No comma when it restricts the noun it follows; a comma in the nonrestrictive use. Never a semicolon, and it cannot open a sentence except as a direct question.
entries.meaning: Means to which, and in its older sense to what end. It is the destination relative, matching thereto ("to it") in the legal there- family and whither among the archaic direction words. American drafting kept the there- member and let this one go: a modern contract says the exhibits attached thereto, never whereto, and ordinary prose says to which.
examples: This is the schedule whereto the exhibits are attached.
The office whereto he was appointed had stood vacant for the better part of a year.
Whereto serves mercy but to confront the visage of offence? (Shakespeare, "Hamlet")
The end whereto all this labor tended was never once explained to the men.
He named in his will the fund whereunto the residue of the estate should fall.

entries.clause: sentence-relative clause of immediate sequence
entries.pattern: [clause], whereupon [clause].
entries.punctuation: A comma before it, never a period. Because it is a relative, it must stay attached to the clause it refers back to; putting a period in front of it creates a fragment. Use thereupon if you want to start a new sentence.
entries.meaning: Means immediately after which — it chains a second event onto the first and implies that the first triggered it. It is fully alive in formal narrative, judicial fact-recitals, and meeting minutes. The distinction that matters: whereupon joins clauses and cannot begin a sentence, whereas its there- twin thereupon is an ordinary adverb and can.
examples: The alarm sounded, whereupon the entire floor emptied in under ninety seconds.
He handed over the envelope, whereupon the officers arrested him on the spot.
The motion was seconded, whereupon the chair called for a vote.
She announced that she was leaving, whereupon the room went completely quiet.
The deposit clears on Friday, whereupon title passes to the buyer.

entries.clause: relative clause of means, usually followed by to + infinitive
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] wherewith to [verb]. · [noun phrase] wherewith [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma — it restricts the noun it follows.
variants: wherewithal (the surviving noun: the wherewithal to pay)
entries.meaning: Means with which or by means of which, and it almost always names the resource somebody lacks (no money wherewith to pay the fine). The word has effectively been replaced by its own derivative: the noun wherewithal, meaning the means or money to do something, is ordinary modern English, while wherewith itself is confined to scripture and period prose.
examples: They had no money wherewith to pay the fine.
He lacked the words wherewith to answer her.
If the salt has lost its savor, wherewith shall it be salted? (after the King James Bible)
She was given a small allowance wherewith to furnish the house.
The trust provides the funds wherewith the school is maintained.

entries.clause: relative clause of destination, or interrogative noun clause
entries.pattern: Whither [clause], [main clause]. · [noun phrase] whither [clause]. · [verb of knowing/saying] whither [clause]. · Whither [noun phrase]?
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted whither clause. No comma when it restricts a noun, and none before an indirect question (no one knew whither the caravan had turned). The headline formula Whither X? is a verbless sentence and takes only its question mark. Never a semicolon.
entries.meaning: Means to where or to which — the direction word matching whence (from where) and where (at where). It survives in two places: the King James Bible (Whither thou goest, I will go) and the headline formula Whither X?, meaning "where is X headed?" Note the pronunciation trap — it is /ˈwɪðər/ with a voiced th, a near-homophone of wither, and the two are constantly confused in print.
examples: Whither thou goest, I will go. (King James Bible)
No one in the camp knew whither the caravan had turned.
Whither American democracy, now that the compromise has collapsed?
He followed the path whither it led, without much hope.
They were bound for a town whither none of them had ever traveled.

entries.clause: sentence-relative connective of consequence — points back at the whole statement before it
entries.pattern: [clause], by reason whereof [clause]. · [clause]; by reason whereof, [clause].
entries.punctuation: A comma before it when it stays welded to the clause it points back at, exactly as with whereupon; a semicolon when the drafter wants two heavier clauses kept apart. Because it contains the relative whereof it cannot open a sentence — for that you need by reason thereof or plain therefore.
entries.meaning: Old pleading language for by reason of which: it names the facts just recited as the cause of the damage about to be claimed, which is why it lives in the damages paragraph of a common-law complaint. It is the where- relative whereof frozen inside a longer phrase. Modern American pleading writes as a result, and only form books and older reports keep the full formula.
examples: The defendant failed to maintain the stairway, by reason whereof the plaintiff fell and was grievously injured.
The vessel was unseaworthy at the time of sailing, by reason whereof the cargo was wholly lost.
No notice was ever given to the surety, by reason whereof the bond is discharged.
The tenant suffered the premises to fall into ruin, by reason whereof the lease became forfeit.
The contract was procured by fraud; by reason whereof, the plaintiff prays that it be rescinded and the consideration returned.

entries.clause: sentence adverbial of instrument; marks its own clause as the act rather than a report of the act
entries.pattern: [subject] hereby [performative verb] [object]. · [subject] is hereby [past participle]. · [noun phrase] herein / hereto / hereof / hereunder — the same here- slot with a different preposition.
entries.punctuation: No commas — hereby sits between the subject and its verb, or between is and the participle, and is never set off. This is exactly where it parts company with thereby, which takes a comma before it when it heads a trailing participial phrase. Never a semicolon: it connects nothing and cannot join two independent clauses.
entries.meaning: The here- family is the mirror of the there- family under therefor: here- plus a preposition means that preposition plus this document. Herein is in this agreement, hereto is to this agreement, hereunder is under this agreement. Hereby is the odd one and the important one, because it means by this very document and is what makes an instrument operate instead of merely describe: I hereby convey performs the conveyance, while I convey only reports one. American plain-language guides tell drafters to delete most of the family and write in this Agreement rather than herein, but they defend hereby in the operative verb, because there the word is doing legal work. One structural difference from the there- family is worth holding on to: here- words point at the paper, so they can open a document, while therefor and thereby point backward at an antecedent and cannot.
examples: The Seller hereby conveys to the Buyer all right, title, and interest in the Property.
Notice of termination is hereby given, effective thirty days from the date written above.
I hereby certify that the foregoing is a true and correct copy of the original.
The parties hereby waive any right to a jury trial in any action arising out of this Agreement.
The obligations described herein survive the closing, and the exhibits attached hereto form part of this Agreement.
The Executive Committee is hereby authorized to negotiate a lease on the terms set out below.

entries.clause: adverbial pro-form meaning later in this document; most often inside a defining parenthetical
entries.pattern: [full name] (hereinafter "[short name]"). · [full name] (hereinafter referred to as "[short name]"). · the [noun] described hereinafter.
entries.punctuation: No commas around it inside a defining parenthetical — (hereinafter "the Buyer") — and none when it modifies a verb. The defined term itself takes quotation marks. Never a semicolon: it connects nothing.
entries.meaning: Here- plus in plus after: from this point on in this document. Its real work in American drafting is not direction but definition — it is the word that christens a party or a term for the rest of the instrument. Keep it apart from hereafter, which means from this time forward in the world rather than from this point on in the paper, and from its backward-looking twin hereinbefore. Plain-language drafters delete it and write (the "Seller"), which does the same job with nothing lost.
examples: Ada Reyes, of Multnomah County, Oregon (hereinafter "the Seller"), agrees to convey the property described below.
Northline Freight, Inc. (hereinafter referred to as "the Carrier") shall maintain insurance in the amounts set out in Schedule C.
The rules of construction set forth hereinafter govern the interpretation of this Agreement.
The Association (hereinafter "the HOA") may levy assessments as provided in Article VIII.
Each of the foregoing is hereinafter referred to individually as a "Party" and collectively as the "Parties."

entries.clause: adverbial pro-form meaning earlier in this document
entries.pattern: the [noun] hereinbefore [past participle]. · as hereinbefore [provided / described / set forth]. · except as hereinbefore provided, [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No commas — it sits directly in front of the participle it modifies (the sum hereinbefore mentioned) and is never set off. Never a semicolon.
entries.meaning: Earlier in this instrument — the backward-looking mate of hereinafter. Three words in this family are swapped constantly and mean three different things: hereinbefore points earlier in the paper, heretofore points earlier than now, and theretofore points earlier than some other past moment. American plain-drafting guides retire all three in favor of above and a section number, but they survive in deeds, wills, and older form books.
examples: The sum hereinbefore mentioned shall be paid on the first day of each month.
Subject to the conditions hereinbefore set forth, the Grantor conveys the land to the Grantee in fee simple.
The Trustee shall hold the property upon the trusts hereinbefore declared.
Except as hereinbefore provided, no waiver of any covenant shall be effective unless made in writing.
The parties hereinbefore named have executed this instrument on the day and year first above written.

entries.clause: sentence adverbial of immediate sequence (= immediately after this)
entries.pattern: [clause]. Hereupon [clause]. · [clause]; hereupon, [clause]. · Hereupon [subject] [verb].
entries.punctuation: A semicolon or a period before it when it stands between two independent clauses; a comma there is a comma splice. A comma after it is optional. It is not the relative whereupon and must not be welded to the previous clause with a comma.
variants: thereupon (the commoner form, pointing back at a past event)
entries.meaning: The third member of the upon trio: whereupon is the relative that has to stay attached to the clause before it, thereupon points back at a past event, and hereupon points at this moment — the one the narrator has just brought the reader to. That deictic here is why it is the rarest of the three: it wants a narrator standing in the scene, which is how Bunyan, Milton, and the eighteenth-century pamphleteers use it. In a modern American document it is essentially never the right word.
examples: The messenger delivered his letter. Hereupon the whole council fell to arguing at once. (18th-century narrative)
He confessed the debt in open court; hereupon the plaintiff moved for judgment.
Hereupon the pilgrim laid down his burden and wept aloud. (after Bunyan)
The bell was rung twice. Hereupon, the doors were shut and no one else admitted.
She refused outright to sign the paper; hereupon the notary declined to proceed.

entries.type: quasi-coordinator — prepositional connective; not a clause introducer
entries.clause: prepositional phrase of substitution (= instead of) modifying the main clause
entries.pattern: [main clause] in lieu of [noun phrase / -ing form]. · In lieu of [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [noun] in lieu of [noun].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted in lieu of phrase; no comma when it trails, which is the ordinary case. Never a semicolon. Note the shape of the phrase: American English requires the of — bare in lieu is British and reads as an error here.
entries.meaning: French lieu is "place," so in lieu of X is in the place of X: one thing is given and another withheld. It is ordinary formal English in American business and legal writing, where it also names specific transactions — deed in lieu of foreclosure, payment in lieu of taxes, pay in lieu of notice. Watch the trap: it means instead of, never in light of, and using it for "in view of" is a common and conspicuous mistake.
examples: The employee received four weeks' pay in lieu of notice.
In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the county library.
The borrower offered the bank a deed in lieu of foreclosure rather than fight the case for a year.
The university will accept a portfolio in lieu of the standard entrance examination.
The town receives an annual payment in lieu of taxes from the hospital.
In lieu of a jury trial, the parties agreed to submit the dispute to a single arbitrator.

entries.type: sentence adverbial (fixed legal formula) — not a conjunction
entries.clause: attestation formula opening the execution clause of an instrument
entries.pattern: IN WITNESS WHEREOF, [parties] have executed this [instrument] as of [date]. · IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand and seal.
entries.punctuation: Conventionally set in capitals and closed by a comma; nothing separates WITNESS from WHEREOF. It opens the last paragraph of the document, immediately above the signature lines. Never a semicolon.
variants: in witness thereof (an error — the formula takes whereof)
entries.meaning: In witness of which — the closing formula of nearly every American contract, deed, will, and certificate, matching know all men by these presents at the top and witnesseth before the recitals. The whereof points back at the entire instrument: the signatures are offered as evidence of everything above them. Plain-language drafters replace it with a bare Signatures heading, but form books and county recorders keep it in circulation.
examples: IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the parties have executed this Agreement as of the date first written above.
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand and affixed my official seal this ninth day of June.
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the Grantor has signed and sealed this deed on the day and year first above written.
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the undersigned has caused this certificate to be executed by its duly authorized officer.
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I set my hand this day and declare this instrument to be my last will and testament.
related: know all men by these presents

entries.ipa: /ɪnˈkludɪŋ bʌt nɑt ˈlɪmɪtɪd tu/, /ɪnˈkludɪŋ bət nɑt ˈlɪmɪtɪd tə/
entries.type: quasi-coordinator — prepositional connective introducing a nonexhaustive list
entries.clause: prepositional phrase of exemplification attached to the general noun before it
entries.pattern: [general noun], including but not limited to, [examples]. · [general noun] including without limitation [examples]. · [general noun], including, but not limited to, [examples].
entries.punctuation: A comma before it when the list is an aside on a noun already complete in itself, and a matching comma after the whole list — the closing comma is the one drafters forget. No commas at all when the phrase is welded into a defined term. Never a semicolon before it; when the listed items themselves contain commas, the items are divided by semicolons.
variants: including but not limited to the following
entries.meaning: The drafter's insurance policy: it announces that the examples to follow do not exhaust the general word in front of them. Lawyers write it because of ejusdem generis, the canon that reads a general term as limited to things like the specific ones listed, and the phrase exists to defeat that reading. Against inter alia, which merely reports that a list is incomplete, this one instructs the reader to take it as incomplete. Plain-language authorities point out that a bare including already means this; American drafters keep writing the long form anyway.
examples: The Tenant shall be responsible for all utilities, including but not limited to water, sewer, gas, and electricity.
The Company may terminate for cause, including but not limited to fraud, theft, or willful misconduct.
Damages of every kind, including without limitation lost profits and loss of goodwill, are excluded by this Section.
The permit covers commercial vehicles including but not limited to trailers, tractors, and semitrailers.
All intellectual property, including but not limited to patents, trademarks, copyrights, and trade secrets, passes to the Buyer at closing.
related: without limiting the generality of the foregoing

entries.term: know all men by these presents
entries.type: performative formula (imperative clause) — not a conjunction
entries.clause: attestation formula opening a deed, bond, or power of attorney; followed by a that clause
entries.pattern: KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS, that [clause]. · KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS: [clause]. · KNOW ALL PERSONS BY THESE PRESENTS, that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Conventionally capitalized and closed by a comma before the that clause, or by a colon. No punctuation inside the formula itself. It opens the instrument, so nothing precedes it and it never takes a semicolon.
variants: know all persons by these presents (the modern degendered form)
know all men whom these presents may concern
to all to whom these presents shall come
entries.meaning: The old opener of a deed, bond, or power of attorney, matching in witness whereof at the foot of the page. These presents means this present document — presents is a noun here, from the legal French ces présentes, and has nothing to do with gifts — so the whole formula is an imperative addressed to the world: let everyone know, by this document, that …. American practice has largely degendered it to KNOW ALL PERSONS BY THESE PRESENTS or dropped it altogether, but it still opens surety bonds and powers of attorney.
examples: KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS, that I, Owen Pike, of Suffolk County, do hereby appoint Ada Reyes my true and lawful attorney-in-fact.
KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS, that we, the Principal and the Surety, are held and firmly bound unto the State of Ohio in the sum of fifty thousand dollars.
KNOW ALL PERSONS BY THESE PRESENTS, that the Grantor, for value received, conveys the land described in Exhibit A.
KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS: the undersigned releases all claims arising out of the collision of March 3.
KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS, that the above-named obligor is firmly bound as set forth below.

entries.clause: sentence adverbial marking the transition from recitals to operative provisions
entries.pattern: NOW, THEREFORE, in consideration of [X], the parties agree as follows: · NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Conventionally set in capitals with a comma after NOW and a comma after THEREFORE, then a comma closing the consideration phrase that follows. The recital immediately before it ends with a semicolon, not a period.
entries.meaning: The hinge of a contract or resolution: it closes the stack of WHEREAS recitals and opens the part that actually binds. It is therefore with a ceremonial now attached, and it works as a structural signpost rather than a genuine logical inference — nothing in the recitals really entails what follows.
examples: NOW, THEREFORE, in consideration of the mutual covenants set forth herein, the parties agree as follows:
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Board authorizes the President to execute the lease.
Now, therefore, the Seller conveys to the Buyer all right, title, and interest in the Property.
Now, therefore, in reliance on the representations set out above, the Lender agrees to extend the maturity date to June 30.
NOW, THEREFORE, for good and valuable consideration, the receipt of which is hereby acknowledged, the parties covenant as follows:

entries.type: quasi-coordinator — prepositional connective; not a clause introducer
entries.clause: prepositional phrase of source or authority modifying the main clause
entries.pattern: Per [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] per [noun phrase]. · As per [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted per phrase; no comma when it trails the clause.
variants: per annum, per diem, per capita (the distributive sense)
entries.meaning: Two jobs. The old distributive one is for each (five percent per annum). The connective one, borrowed from legal Latin, is according to — per our conversation, per Section 12 — and this is the one that dominates American business email. The expanded as per is entrenched but widely disliked as redundant; per alone, or plain according to, is safer in anything that will be read closely.
examples: Per our conversation this morning, I have attached the revised estimate.
The flooring was installed per the manufacturer's written instructions.
As per your request, the meeting has been moved to Thursday afternoon.
Interest accrues at five percent per annum on the unpaid balance.
Per Section 12, notice of termination must be given in writing.

entries.type: quasi-coordinator — prepositional connective; not a clause introducer
entries.clause: prepositional phrase of authority modifying the main clause
entries.pattern: Pursuant to [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] pursuant to [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted pursuant to phrase; no comma when it trails the clause.
entries.meaning: Means under the authority of or in accordance with, and it is the standard way an American lawyer cites the rule that licenses an action (pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6)). Against per, which is loose and commercial, pursuant to is precise and points at a specific legal instrument. Plain-language drafting guides recommend replacing it with under, and courts increasingly do.
examples: Pursuant to Section 8 of the Agreement, the Buyer hereby gives notice of termination.
The records were released pursuant to a valid and properly served subpoena.
Pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6), the defendant moves to dismiss the complaint in its entirety.
The search was conducted pursuant to a warrant issued that same morning.
Pursuant to the court's order of May 4, the parties have conferred in good faith.

entries.type: quasi-coordinator — prepositional connective; not a clause introducer
entries.clause: prepositional phrase of condition or subordination modifying the main clause
entries.pattern: Subject to [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause], subject to [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted subject to phrase. A trailing one takes a comma only when it qualifies the whole clause as an afterthought (The merger will close on October 1, subject to the Board's approval); it takes no comma when it is part of the predicate, which is the commoner case (The offer is subject to financing). Never a semicolon. Note the stress: the connective is SUB-ject, first syllable, unlike the verb sub-JECT.
variants: without prejudice to (a near-synonym in drafting)
entries.meaning: The mirror image of notwithstanding: subject to Section 4 means Section 4 wins, while notwithstanding Section 4 means this clause wins. That single pair does most of the work of resolving conflicts between provisions in an American contract, and reversing them inverts the deal. In ordinary use it simply means conditional on (subject to financing).
examples: Subject to Section 4, the Company shall reimburse all reasonable travel expenses.
The offer is subject to financing and to a satisfactory inspection.
Subject to the Board's approval, the merger will close on October 1.
All payments under this Agreement are subject to withholding required by applicable law.
The lease is subject to the rights of the existing tenants.

entries.type: anaphoric adverb of source — not a conjunction
entries.register: archaic and literary in prose; fully alive in deeds and surveys
entries.clause: adverbial pro-form meaning from there / from that; continues a route or a chain of reasoning
entries.pattern: [clause], thence to [place]. · [clause] and thence [direction / prepositional phrase]. · THENCE [bearing] [distance] to [monument] (survey call). · [clause]; thence [clause] (the old inferential sense).
entries.punctuation: A comma or and before it when it continues an itinerary (they sailed to Lisbon, thence to Tangier). In a metes-and-bounds description each thence opens a new leg and the legs are divided by semicolons, with no comma after the word itself. It is not a conjunction, so it cannot join two independent clauses on a comma — that is a comma splice, exactly as it would be with therefore; use a semicolon or a period.
variants: from thence (long established, though strictly redundant)
entries.meaning: The demonstrative member of the little set that whence and whither belong to: whence is from where, hence is from here, thence is from there. The from is already inside the word, which makes from thence a redundancy of exactly the same kind as from whence — and, since the King James translators wrote it too, exactly as long established. Two lives survive in American English. In literary and travel prose it chains an itinerary (to Denver, and thence to the coast). In land law it is not archaic at all: every metes-and-bounds description in an American deed is a chain of thence calls, and a title examiner reads dozens in a working week. A third, faded sense — from that it follows — has been handed over to hence.
examples: They sailed first to Lisbon, thence to Tangier.
The family moved to Chicago in 1911 and thence to Detroit two years later.
THENCE North 12 degrees East a distance of 210.5 feet to an iron pin; THENCE South 78 degrees East 96 feet to the point of beginning. (deed description)
Water is pumped to the reservoir on the hill and thence to every house in the valley.
The trail climbs to the ridge, thence down into the next valley.
The premise is granted; thence the conclusion follows without further argument. (the old inferential sense; modern English says "hence")

entries.clause: sentence adverbial of result; most often heads a participial phrase
entries.pattern: [clause], thereby [-ing phrase]. · [clause] and thereby [verb phrase]. · [clause]; thereby [clause].
entries.punctuation: When it heads a participial phrase, put a comma before thereby and none after it (…, thereby cutting the commute). When it joins two independent clauses on its own, it needs a semicolon before it, like any conjunctive adverb.
entries.meaning: Means by that means — it names the mechanism by which the main clause produced its effect. Its favorite construction by far is a trailing participle (thereby reducing errors), which is also where writers get into trouble: the participle must attach to the subject of the main clause, or you have a dangling modifier. Distinguish hereby, which means by this very document and is what makes a legal instrument operate (I hereby convey).
examples: The city widened the road, thereby cutting the average commute by six minutes.
She signed the release, thereby giving up any claim to the property.
He missed the filing deadline and thereby forfeited the appeal.
The deed was recorded on Monday; thereby the buyer's title became a matter of public record.
Automating the intake form eliminated three handoffs, thereby reducing errors by roughly half.

entries.type: anaphoric pro-adverb — not a true conjunction
entries.clause: adverbial pro-form standing for preposition + it/that; binds the clause to something already named
