entries.pattern: [noun phrase] therefor (= for it / for that). · [verb] [object] therefor. · [noun phrase] thereto / therein / thereof / thereunder — the same slot with a different preposition.
entries.punctuation: No commas — these words attach directly to what they modify and are never set off.
entries.meaning: A whole family of legal pro-adverbs: there- plus a preposition, meaning that preposition plus it or that. Therefor is for it, thereto is to it, therein is in it, thereunder is under it. They are not conjunctions, but they do a conjunction's cohesive work, tying each clause back to an antecedent without repeating it. Watch the stress: therefor (thair-FOR, = for it) and therefore (THAIR-fore, = consequently) differ by one letter and one stress, and swapping them changes the meaning of a sentence entirely.
examples: The Contractor shall supply all materials and submit a single invoice therefor.
If the equipment is damaged, the Lessee shall pay the reasonable cost of repair therefor.
This Agreement, together with all exhibits thereto, constitutes the entire understanding of the parties.
The Landlord shall maintain the building and all mechanical systems therein.
The Company grants the license and shall receive the royalty provided therefor in Schedule B.

entries.clause: adverbial pro-form of time meaning before that time, anchored to a past reference point rather than to now
entries.pattern: [past-tense clause] theretofore [past participle]. · the [noun] theretofore [held / paid / existing]. · [main clause], as theretofore provided.
entries.punctuation: No commas — it sits directly before the participle or verb it modifies, like the rest of the there- family. Never a semicolon.
variants: up to that time (the plain equivalent)
entries.meaning: Before that time — the past-anchored twin of heretofore, which means before now. The distinction is the whole reason the word exists: in a narrative or a set of findings that has already moved into the past, heretofore would wrongly reach back from the present day, while theretofore reaches back only as far as the moment under discussion. It survives in judicial opinions, deeds, and older statutes; plain-language drafters write previously or before then.
examples: On March 3 the company canceled the policy that had theretofore covered the entire fleet.
The court set aside the judgment theretofore entered against the surety.
The parties abandoned the practice theretofore followed in settling their accounts.
She took possession of the farm, which had theretofore belonged to her uncle.
All sums theretofore advanced became due and payable upon the default.

entries.clause: sentence adverbial of immediate sequence or consequence
entries.pattern: [clause]. Thereupon, [clause]. · [clause]; thereupon [clause]. · [clause] and thereupon [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: As a conjunctive adverb it takes a semicolon or period before it; a comma after it is optional. A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
entries.meaning: Means immediately after that or on that basis. It is the free-standing twin of whereupon, and the difference is purely syntactic: whereupon is a relative and must stay welded to the previous clause with a comma, while thereupon is an ordinary adverb and can open a brand-new sentence.
examples: The chairman ruled the motion out of order. Thereupon, three members walked out.
She named her price; thereupon the negotiation ended.
The check cleared on Thursday, and thereupon the deed was recorded.
He confessed in full. Thereupon the investigation was closed.
The court found the contract void and thereupon dismissed the suit.

entries.clause: sentence adverbial of accompaniment or immediate sequence (= with that, thereupon, besides)
entries.pattern: [clause]; therewithal [clause]. · [clause], and therewithal [verb phrase]. · [clause]. Therewithal, [clause].
entries.punctuation: A semicolon or a period before it when it joins two independent clauses, exactly as with thereupon; a comma alone there is a comma splice. After and it takes no punctuation at all, which is its commonest position in period prose.
entries.meaning: There + with + all: with that, and by extension thereupon and besides. Period writers slide between two senses — the instrumental (he drew his sword and therewithal cut the rope) and the additive (she was clever, and therewithal kind) — and the reader has to take the sense from the context. Chaucer, Malory, and the King James translators use it; the modern words are with that, thereupon, and besides.
examples: He drew a letter from his coat, and therewithal a small brass key.
She was quick and clever, and therewithal kinder than anyone else in that house.
The steward brought in bread and wine; therewithal he set a dish of olives on the board.
He gave his promise, and therewithal his hand upon it.
The storm broke a little after midnight; therewithal every light along the quay went out.

entries.term: without limiting the generality of the foregoing
entries.ipa: /wɪˌðaʊt ˈlɪmɪtɪŋ ðə ˌdʒɛnəˈrælɪti əv ðə fɔrˈɡoʊɪŋ/
entries.respell: with-OWT LIM-it-ing thuh jen-uh-RAL-uh-tee uhv thuh for-GOH-ing
entries.clause: sentence adverbial tying a specific provision back to the general one before it
entries.pattern: [general provision]. Without limiting the generality of the foregoing, [specific provision]. · [general provision]; without limiting the generality of the foregoing, [specific provision].
entries.punctuation: A period or a semicolon before it and a comma after it. It stands between two independent clauses, so a comma alone in front of it is a comma splice, exactly as with however. In numbered drafting it usually opens its own subsection.
variants: without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing (the British form)
entries.meaning: The long-form cousin of including but not limited to: it lets a drafter give one specific instance of a general obligation without the reader concluding that the general words have been cut down to that instance. Like the shorter phrase it exists to defeat ejusdem generis, the canon that reads general language as limited by the specifics attached to it. Plain-language authorities treat it as one of the worst mouthfuls in American drafting, and the honest replacements are for example or a separate numbered clause.
examples: The Contractor shall comply with all applicable law. Without limiting the generality of the foregoing, the Contractor shall obtain every permit required by the county before work begins.
Tenant shall keep the premises in good repair; without limiting the generality of the foregoing, Tenant shall have the heating system serviced twice each year.
The Lender may take any action it deems necessary to protect the collateral. Without limiting the generality of the foregoing, it may take possession of the equipment without prior notice.
Each party shall keep the other's information confidential. Without limiting the generality of the foregoing, neither party shall disclose the pricing terms to any competitor.
The Seller makes no representation of any kind; without limiting the generality of the foregoing, the Seller disclaims all implied warranties of merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose.

entries.type: archaic verb form used as a formulaic heading — not a conjunction
entries.clause: structural heading standing between the parties clause and the recitals
entries.pattern: THIS [instrument], made [date], between [parties], WITNESSETH: · THIS [instrument] WITNESSETH that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Conventionally capitalized and followed by a colon when it heads the recitals, or by that when it runs straight into the operative language. No comma before it.
entries.meaning: The third-person singular present of witness with the old -eth ending — literally "this document bears witness." It is not a conjunction, but it sits in the connective slot of a deed or indenture, immediately before the WHEREAS recitals, which is why it belongs alongside them. Modern American drafting has largely replaced it with a plain Background or Recitals heading, but it survives in deeds, trust instruments, and form books.
examples: THIS INDENTURE, made this tenth day of April, between Ada Reyes and Owen Pike, WITNESSETH:
THIS AGREEMENT WITNESSETH that, in consideration of the sum of one dollar, the Grantor conveys the land described below.
THIS TRUST AGREEMENT WITNESSETH: That the Settlor hereby transfers to the Trustee the property described in Schedule A.
THIS BILL OF SALE WITNESSETH that the Seller, for value received, sells and delivers the goods listed below.
THIS LEASE, between the Landlord and the Tenant named above, WITNESSETH as follows:

entries.clause: adverbial clause of condition
entries.pattern: An [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], an [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted an clause. A comma before a trailing one is usual, but that follows the loose comma practice of the period rather than the modern rule, which leaves a trailing conditional clause unpunctuated (I will do it if you wish it). In modernized editions it is often printed an' with an apostrophe. Never a semicolon.
variants: and (the older spelling of the same word)
entries.meaning: The archaic conditional if, everywhere in Shakespeare and Middle English (an it please your honor). It is the same word as the coordinating and, which once carried a conditional sense too — the fossil survives in and if and in dialect. Do not confuse it with the article an: the article precedes a noun, this precedes a whole clause.
examples: An it please your honor, I shall wait outside. (Shakespeare-era usage)
I will do it, an you wish it.
An he be a true knight, he will keep his word.
Come tomorrow, an you can.
He would speak plainly, an he dared.

entries.type: quasi-coordinator — prepositional connective; not a clause introducer
entries.register: archaic; chiefly Scots and Scottish legal
entries.clause: prepositional phrase of topic (= concerning, about) modifying the main clause
entries.pattern: Anent [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] anent [noun phrase]. · [noun of writing or speech] anent [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted anent phrase; no comma when it trails the clause. Never a semicolon — it takes a noun phrase, not a clause.
entries.meaning: Means concerning or about. It is Scots and northern English rather than general archaic English, and an American meets it in Walter Scott, in Burns, in Scottish court reports and kirk-session records, and in the deliberately antique voice of nineteenth-century correspondence. Against as touching, the King James Bible's phrase for the same job, anent is legal and epistolary; both are dead in American prose, where concerning or plain about is the only live choice.
examples: I have your letter anent the disputed march between our two farms. (19th-century Scottish correspondence)
The Session has taken no action anent the complaint laid before it in March. (kirk-session records)
Anent the matter of the entail, my client will say nothing further at present.
He held views anent the education of women that scandalized the whole parish.
The Sheriff pronounced an interlocutor anent the expenses of the cause. (Scots legal usage)
Anent your inquiry of the twelfth, the books were sold at Edinburgh in 1843.

entries.type: quasi-coordinator — prepositional connective; not a clause introducer
entries.clause: prepositional phrase of topic (= concerning, as regards) modifying the main clause
entries.pattern: As touching [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] as touching [noun phrase]. · Touching [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after the fronted phrase, which is where it nearly always sits; no comma when it trails the clause. Never a semicolon.
entries.meaning: The King James Bible's way of announcing a change of subject: As touching the resurrection of the dead, have ye not read …. All three members of the set are participial prepositions — touching is the present participle of touch pressed into service exactly as concerning and regarding were — and as concerning and the bare touching do the same work. An American meets them in scripture, in Shakespeare, and in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century correspondence; the modern equivalents are concerning, as for, and when it comes to.
examples: Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. (King James Bible)
As touching the resurrection of the dead, have ye not read that which was spoken unto you by God? (King James Bible)
Touching the matter of the lease, I have written to Mr. Havisham this morning.
As concerning the sum advanced last Michaelmas, no account has yet been rendered.
He would say nothing whatever as touching his own part in the affair.
Touching your request for leave, the Colonel has returned no answer.

entries.clause: sentence adverbial of immediate sequence or repetition (= soon afterward, again)
entries.pattern: [clause]. Eftsoons [clause]. · [clause], and eftsoons [verb phrase]. · [clause]; eftsoons [clause].
entries.punctuation: As a sentence adverb it takes a semicolon or a period before it when it stands between two independent clauses, exactly like thereupon; a comma there is a comma splice. No comma after it in verse, where it usually sits inside the line.
entries.meaning: Old English eft ("again") plus soon: soon afterward, or simply again. It was already antique when Spenser revived it for The Faerie Queene, and Coleridge took it from Spenser for the line most American readers know it by — Eftsoons his hand dropt he, in "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner." You will meet it there, in Spenser, and essentially nowhere else; thereupon is the living word for the same job.
examples: Eftsoons his hand dropt he. (Coleridge, "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner")
The knight rode forth at daybreak, and eftsoons came to a darksome wood. (after Spenser)
She rebuked him sharply; eftsoons he was begging her pardon.
Eftsoons the trumpet sounded a second time, and the lists were cleared.
He swore he would never come back to that house, yet eftsoons he was at the gate again.

entries.type: subordinating; also prepositional before a noun phrase
entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (anteriority)
entries.pattern: Ere [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] ere [clause]. · ere [noun phrase].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted ere clause; no comma when it follows the main clause — exactly like before.
entries.meaning: Simply before, in time. It is the standard poetic and scriptural form and is common in hymns, carols, and nineteenth-century verse. Three near-homophones cause trouble: ere (before), e'er (a contraction of ever), and air are all /ɛr/ in American English, and err (to make a mistake) is close enough to add to the confusion.
examples: Ere the sun sets, we shall be home.
He was gone ere I could thank him.
Ere long the whole town knew every detail.
Many a night I have watched the harbor ere the boats came in.
She died ere the letter ever reached her.
Ere you go, take this with you.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of negative condition (= unless)
entries.pattern: Except [subject] [bare verb], [main clause]. · [main clause] except [subject] [bare verb].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted except clause; no comma when it trails the main clause, exactly as with unless. The verb is in the bare subjunctive: except he repent, not except he repents. Never a semicolon.
entries.meaning: This is the archaic except meaning unless, not the everyday one meaning apart from. It is the King James Bible's standard negative conditional — Except a man be born again, Except ye repent — and it takes the subjunctive as reliably as lest does. The modern exceptive sense is a separate entry, except that. Three word classes share the spelling: preposition (everyone except me), verb (present company excepted), and conjunction — and the conjunction itself splits in two, the archaic unless of this entry and the ordinary except that.
examples: Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. (King James Bible)
Except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it. (King James Bible)
Except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. (King James Bible)
I will not go except you come with me.
No one may enter the hall except he bear the seal of the order.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of cause
entries.pattern: [main clause] for that [clause]. · For that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], for that [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma when it restricts the main clause; a comma when it comments on the whole of it. Comma after a fronted for that clause. Never a semicolon.
variants: for (the coordinator it is built on)
entries.meaning: The Early Modern English because, built from the causal for plus the complementizer that — the same recipe that gave French parce que and Spanish porque. Shakespeare and the King James translators use it freely; it went out with the seventeenth century and left behind its narrower relative in that, which kept the construction but restricted it from plain cause to cause-in-a-specified-respect. Do not read it as the preposition for plus the demonstrative that (this envelope is for that client): the conjunction is followed by an entire clause, never by a noun.
examples: He was punished for that he had spoken against the king.
For that the night was bitterly cold, they built the fire high and kept a watch.
The men gave thanks, for that the ship had come safely into harbor.
She would not open the door, for that she knew not who stood outside.
For that no answer was returned within the term, the suit was taken as confessed.
I love him not, for that he keeps such company.

entries.clause: sentence adverbial of concession; or adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: [clause]. Howbeit, [clause]. · [clause]; howbeit, [clause]. · Howbeit [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: As a sentence adverb it takes a semicolon or period before, comma after, exactly like however. As a subordinator (rarer) it takes a comma after its clause.
variants: how be it (the original three-word form)
entries.meaning: However it may be — that is, nevertheless. It is the exact concessive twin of albeit, built the same way from how + be + it, but where albeit survived into modern formal prose, howbeit died out completely after the seventeenth century. You will meet it in the King James Bible and in Shakespeare's contemporaries and essentially nowhere else.
examples: Howbeit, the ship held together until morning.
He gave his word freely; howbeit, he did not keep it.
Howbeit we did not know it at the time, the decision had already been taken.
Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth. (King James Bible)
She was warned twice. Howbeit, she went alone.

entries.register: dialectal, nonstandard — Southern, Appalachian, and Ozark speech
entries.clause: adverbial clause of negative condition (= unless)
entries.pattern: [main clause] less'n [clause]. · Less'n [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma when it follows the main clause; comma after a fronted less'n clause — the punctuation of unless exactly. In print it keeps the apostrophe, which marks the worn-away un-. Never a semicolon.
variants: without (the same job in the same dialects)
entries.meaning: Unless with the first syllable worn off — heard in Southern, Appalachian, and Ozark speech and used constantly by writers rendering it, from Twain and Joel Chandler Harris through a century of American dialect fiction. It is not archaic literary English and not available for ordinary writing: outside dialogue an American writes unless. It runs in harness with the conjunction without (= unless), the other nonstandard exceptive of the same regions.
examples: I ain't going in there less'n you come with me.
He won't say a word about it less'n you ask him twice.
Less'n the rain holds off, there'll be no hay cut this week.
Don't you open that gate less'n I tell you to.
She'd never have known a thing about it less'n somebody told her.
There's no getting up that road less'n you've got chains on the tires.

entries.type: quasi-coordinator — prepositional connective; not a clause introducer
entries.clause: concessive prepositional phrase (= in spite of)
entries.pattern: Maugre [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] maugre [noun phrase]. · maugre [possessive] teeth (the fixed old idiom).
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted maugre phrase; no comma when it trails. Never a semicolon — it takes a noun phrase, never a clause.
entries.meaning: From Old French maugré, "ill will" — literally in the teeth of, hence in spite of. Chaucer, Spenser, and Milton use it freely, and it kept one fossilized idiom for centuries: maugre his teeth, meaning "against his will, whatever he could do about it." It is a preposition and not a conjunction, and notwithstanding is the word that took over its work in modern formal English.
examples: Maugre all his oaths, he was back in the tavern by nightfall.
She would have her way maugre her father and her uncles both.
Maugre his teeth, the knight was carried from the field. (the fixed old idiom)
The town held out maugre famine, fire, and three assaults in a single week.
Maugre the storm, the packet sailed on the evening tide.

entries.clause: sentence adverbial of concession (= nevertheless)
entries.pattern: [clause]; natheless [clause]. · [clause]. Natheless, [clause]. · Natheless [subject] [verb].
entries.punctuation: A semicolon or a period before it, exactly as with nevertheless; a comma alone between the two clauses is a comma splice. A comma after it is optional and is usually dropped in verse for the meter.
variants: ne the less (the original three words)
entries.meaning: Old English ná þe lǽs, "none the less" — the direct ancestor of nevertheless, built with the negative ne where the modern word has never. Milton's Nathless he so endur'd is where most American readers meet it; Spenser and the nineteenth-century medievalists supply the rest. Nothing about it is available for modern use: write nevertheless.
examples: Nathless he so endur'd, till on the beach of that inflamed sea he stood. (Milton, "Paradise Lost")
The night was bitter cold; natheless they kept the watch till dawn.
He was warned twice of the danger. Natheless, he went alone into the wood.
Her fortune was gone; natheless she bore herself as a queen to the end.
Natheless the ship held her course, though the mast was sprung and the pumps were failing.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of cause or of time
entries.pattern: Sith [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] sith [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted sith clause; no comma when it follows — the same rules that govern since.
entries.meaning: The Middle and Early Modern English ancestor of since, and it carries the same double life: because (Sith it is so, let us make the best of it) and from the time that (Much has changed sith last we met). Spenser and Shakespeare use it freely; by the eighteenth century since had taken over completely, and sith survives only as deliberate archaism. Its longer form sithence — sith with the old adverbial -s on the end, respelled -ce — is the same conjunction in fuller dress, and is the form much sixteenth-century prose prefers; it died with the shorter one, which is why it is listed here rather than on its own.
examples: Sith thou art gone, the house is silent.
Sith it is so, let us make the best of it.
Much has changed sith last we met.
Sith the king commands it, we must obey.
He has not spoken a word sith the trial began.
Sithence the Conquest, no such charter hath been granted. (16th-century usage)

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time (immediate anteriority)
entries.pattern: So soon as [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] so soon as [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted so soon as clause; no comma when it follows the main clause — the punctuation of as soon as exactly. Never a semicolon.
entries.meaning: The older form of as soon as, standard through the eighteenth century and still ordinary in Austen, Scott, and the nineteenth-century novel: the so … as frame was the usual English pattern before as … as took it over in positive clauses. It is not an American form today, and in modern prose it reads as period costume rather than formality.
examples: So soon as the letter was written, she carried it herself to the post. (19th-century usage)
He resolved to speak to her so soon as they were left alone.
So soon as the tide serves, the ship will drop down the river.
She knew him for a scoundrel so soon as he opened his mouth.
So soon as the news reached the town, every shop in the street was shut up.

entries.type: emphatic sentence adverb — not a conjunction
entries.clause: discourse-initial sentence adverbial of assertion — vouches for the clause it opens
entries.pattern: Verily [subject] [verb]. · Verily, [clause]. · Verily, verily, I say unto you, [clause].
entries.punctuation: A comma after it in modern typesetting when it opens a sentence; the King James Bible prints Verily I say unto you with no comma at all, and quotations should keep the original pointing. It joins nothing, so nothing precedes it — it opens its own sentence, and a semicolon before it would be wrong.
entries.meaning: Truly, in truth — a swearing-word rather than a connective: it stakes the speaker's credit on what follows. Its home is the King James Gospels, where Verily I say unto you renders the Greek amēn and marks the most solemn sayings; John doubles it. An American meets it there, in hymns, and in the deliberately biblical cadence of nineteenth-century oratory, and in modern speech only as a joke about that cadence.
examples: Verily I say unto you, this generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled. (King James Bible)
Verily, verily, I say unto thee, except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God. (King James Bible)
Verily the man was righteous, and his house prospered after him.
Verily, I have seen the like of it but once in fifty years.
Their cause is just, and verily it shall prevail. (19th-century pulpit oratory)

entries.clause: adverbial clause of time; occasionally of cause or contrast (= whereas)
entries.pattern: Whenas [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] whenas [clause].
entries.punctuation: Comma after a fronted whenas clause, which is where it nearly always sits in verse; no comma when it trails. Never a semicolon.
variants: when that (the same doubling with that)
entries.meaning: When, with the old expletive as welded on — the same doubling that produced whereas, whiles that, and when that, all of them ways of marking a bare adverb unmistakably as a conjunction. It is chiefly Elizabethan and Jacobean, and its most quoted line is Herrick's Whenas in silks my Julia goes. A second and weaker sense, seeing that or whereas, turns up in seventeenth-century prose and in old statutes.
examples: Whenas in silks my Julia goes, then, then, methinks, how sweetly flows that liquefaction of her clothes. (Herrick)
Whenas the sun went down, the watch was set upon the walls.
He was silent whenas the question was put to him directly.
Whenas the King had need of money, a Parliament was called. (17th-century prose)
Whenas they had eaten, the elder rose up and spoke.

entries.clause: adverbial clause of negative condition (= unless)
entries.pattern: [main clause] without [clause]. · Without [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma when it follows the main clause; comma after a fronted without clause.
entries.meaning: The conjunction without, meaning unless, is a different animal from the ordinary preposition. Standard until the eighteenth century, it is now nonstandard in edited American English but alive in Southern and rural speech and used constantly in dialogue by writers rendering it. Test which one you have: the preposition takes a noun phrase (without a coat), the conjunction takes a whole clause (without you come with me). A third class rounds it out — the adverb of place surviving in a sound from without and the view from without — so preposition, adverb, and conjunction all share the one spelling.
examples: I won't go without you come with me.
He'll not lend a dime without he sees the deed first.
Don't you touch that without I tell you to.
Nothing gets planted without the ground thaws first.
She never came into town without it was market day.
Without you sign it yourself, they won't take it at the courthouse.

entries.type: reader-directive cross-reference marker — not a conjunction
entries.clause: stands outside the clause structure; points the reader at a differing or comparable source
entries.pattern: [claim] (cf. [source]). · [claim]; cf. [source]. · Cf. [source], which reaches the opposite conclusion.
entries.punctuation: Written cf. with a single period and no comma after it — this is exactly where it differs from i.e. and e.g., which both require one. It normally sits inside parentheses, a footnote, or a citation sentence of its own, and what follows it is a source, not a restatement.
entries.meaning: Latin confer, the imperative "compare." It tells the reader to look at another source and notice how it differs — not to look up a definition, and not to read an illustration. Two errors are worth heading off: cf. is not an abbreviation of see (that is plain see, or quod vide for a cross-reference inside the same work), and it never takes the comma that i.e. and e.g. require. In American legal citation cf. signals support by analogy, while contra signals the opposite.
examples: Most surveys put the figure near forty percent (cf. Alvarez 2019, who reports twenty-two).
The court applied the same test to municipal employees. Cf. Garcetti v. Ceballos, 547 U.S. 410 (2006).
The manuscript is usually dated to about 1340; cf. Whitfield, who argues for a generation later.
Nesting begins in early April (cf. the coastal population, which begins three weeks sooner).
She treats the 1919 strike as a failure — cf. Reyes, who calls it the beginning of the modern union.

entries.clause: sentence adverbial of logical consequence
entries.pattern: [clause]; ergo, [clause]. · [clause]. Ergo, [clause]. · [premise] — ergo, [conclusion].
entries.punctuation: Like therefore, it needs a semicolon or a period before it when it joins two independent clauses, and it takes a comma after it. A dash before it is common in compressed argument.
entries.meaning: Latin for therefore, and unlike most Latin survivals it is spoken aloud as often as written. It marks a strict logical inference rather than a loose consequence, which gives it two registers at once: perfectly serious in philosophy and law, and mock-pompous everywhere else, where an American reaches for it to signal that the conclusion is meant to be obvious.
examples: The lock was undamaged; ergo, whoever came in had a key.
All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; ergo, Socrates is mortal.
He was not at the meeting. Ergo, he cannot have heard the announcement.
The file was modified after the deadline; ergo, it was not the version submitted.
No fingerprints, no forced entry, nothing missing — ergo, no burglary.

entries.type: quasi-coordinator — abbreviated coordination closing a list of names
entries.clause: closes a noun phrase; stands in for the remaining coordinates of a list of people
entries.pattern: [Name] et al., [year]. · [Name] et al. [verb]. · [Name] v. [Name] et al. (case caption).
entries.punctuation: Written et al. — no period after et, which is a whole Latin word, and one period after al., which is an abbreviation. American style does not italicize it, and it takes no comma before it: Weinberg et al. found, never Weinberg, et al. found. At the end of a sentence its period serves as the full stop as well.
variants: inter alia (a different word — among other things)
entries.meaning: Latin and others, and the only member of this section that actually coordinates: it replaces the second and later names in a list of authors, parties, or defendants. Its confusion with inter alia is worth heading off — et al. stands for people left out of a list of names, while inter alia warns that a list of things is incomplete. Note also that it abbreviates a coordination, not a plural: Weinberg et al. means Weinberg and at least two others, and the verb agrees with the whole group.
examples: Weinberg et al. reported the same effect in a much larger cohort.
The suit names the city, the transit authority, et al. as defendants.
See Okafor et al., "Coastal Subsidence in the Gulf," 2021.
The complaint in Alvarez et al. v. Northline Freight was filed in March.
The grant was awarded jointly to Dr. Pierce et al. at the state laboratory.

entries.clause: appositional phrase introducing an illustrative sample
entries.pattern: [clause] — e.g., [examples]. · [clause] (e.g., [examples]). · [noun phrase], e.g., [examples].
entries.punctuation: American style: a period after each letter and a comma after the whole abbreviation — e.g., — with a comma, a dash, or an opening parenthesis before it. Never close the list with etc., which repeats what e.g. already said.
entries.meaning: Latin for the sake of example, and it introduces a partial list — a sample, with more left unsaid. Its constant confusion with id est is the most common Latin error in American writing: e.g. gives you some of the class, i.e. restates the whole of it. The standard mnemonic is e.g. = example given. Almost nobody says the Latin aloud; readers say "for example" or spell out the letters.
examples: Bring something to write with (e.g., a pen or a sharpened pencil).
The policy covers large durable goods — e.g., refrigerators, washers, and stoves.
Some English verbs take two objects, e.g., give and send.
Please avoid strong solvents, e.g., acetone or lacquer thinner.
Certain fees are nonrefundable (e.g., the application fee).

entries.clause: appositional phrase introducing a restatement of what precedes
entries.pattern: [clause] — i.e., [restatement]. · [clause] (i.e., [restatement]). · [noun phrase], i.e., [restatement].
entries.punctuation: American style: a period after each letter and a comma after the whole abbreviation — i.e., — preceded by a comma, a dash, or an opening parenthesis.
entries.meaning: Latin that is. It introduces a restatement: the same thing said again more precisely, covering the whole of what came before. Against exempli gratia, which offers a sample, i.e. offers an equivalent — the fee is due at signing, i.e., before you get the keys redefines the moment rather than illustrating it. Read it aloud as "that is," not as Latin.
examples: The fee is due at signing — i.e., before you receive the keys.
She works the graveyard shift, i.e., eleven at night to seven in the morning.
Only the principal is refundable (i.e., not the accrued interest).
Please respond by close of business, i.e., five o'clock Eastern time.
The device is rated IP68, i.e., it can be fully submerged without damage.

entries.type: enumerative discourse marker — not a conjunction
entries.clause: opens the first item of a formal enumeration; stands outside the clause it introduces
entries.pattern: Imprimis, [first item]. Item, [second item]. · Imprimis: [first item].
entries.punctuation: Followed by a comma, or by a colon in an inventory, and it opens its own sentence or line. Nothing precedes it — it is by definition the first thing in the list — so the question of a semicolon before it never arises.
variants: item (the marker for every entry after the first)
entries.meaning: Latin in the first place — the opening marker of the old itemized will, inventory, or account, always answered by a string of item entries beneath it. An American meets the pair in probate files, in colonial inventories of estates, and in Shakespeare's parody of the form in Twelfth Night. The modern replacements are a numbered list and the word First.
examples: Imprimis, I give and bequeath unto my wife Elizabeth the dwelling house and the ground thereto belonging. (will, 1698)
Imprimis: one bay mare, with saddle and bridle, valued at eight pounds. (inventory of an estate)
Imprimis, the Committee finds that no notice of the meeting was ever given to the membership.
Imprimis, we are to consider what the statute meant by the word "resident."
Imprimis, two feather beds; item, one iron pot; item, six pewter dishes. (colonial probate inventory)

entries.type: parenthetical adverbial phrase — not a conjunction
entries.clause: parenthetical adverbial meaning among other things; marks the list around it as incomplete
entries.pattern: [verb], inter alia, [object]. · [subject], inter alia, [predicate]. · [noun phrase] (inter alia).
entries.punctuation: Commas on both sides, or a pair of parentheses — it interrupts a clause rather than joining two, and dropping the closing comma is the usual error, the same one that spoils to wit. Never a semicolon, and never a comma on one side only.
entries.meaning: Latin among other things, and in force the exact opposite of videlicet: viz. promises that the enumeration is complete, inter alia warns that it is not. Its home is the brief and the judicial opinion — the court held, inter alia, that the statute was not retroactive — where it lets a writer report one item from a holding without seeming to report the whole of it, a difference that in litigation is substantive rather than stylistic. Two cautions. It is inter alia for things and inter alios for people, and the second is regularly botched. And outside law the plain among other things costs nothing and loses nothing, which is what most American editors will make you write.
examples: The court held, inter alia, that the notice period had never been properly triggered.
The complaint alleges, inter alia, breach of contract and unjust enrichment.
The agency cited, inter alia, the cost of compliance for small carriers.
The report recommends unannounced inspections (inter alia) and a single reporting deadline.
She has advised, inter alios, two former governors and a sitting senator.
The statute applies, inter alia, to trusts created before its effective date.

entries.type: enumerative discourse marker — not a conjunction
entries.clause: opens each entry after the first in a formal enumeration
entries.pattern: Imprimis, [first entry]. Item, [next entry]. Item, [next entry]. · Item: [entry] (inventory or account).
entries.punctuation: Followed by a comma, or by a colon in an account book, and it opens its own line or sentence. The entries are stacked with no connective between them: the repeated Item is the connective, which is why no and ever appears in these lists.
variants: imprimis (the marker for the first entry)
entries.meaning: Latin likewise — the word that opened every entry after the first in a will, inventory, or bill of particulars, and the reason English has the noun an item: the marker for a listed thing became the name of the thing. An American meets the adverb in probate files, colonial account books, and Shakespeare's mockery of the form in Twelfth Night, and meets its descendant the noun everywhere.
examples: Item, I give to my son John my silver watch and my best coat. (will, 1712)
Item, two feather beds; item, one iron pot; item, six pewter dishes. (estate inventory)
Item: to mending the parish gate, three shillings. (churchwarden's accounts)
Item, two lips, indifferent red; item, two grey eyes, with lids to them. (Shakespeare, "Twelfth Night")
Item, the tenant covenants to keep the fences and gates in repair.

entries.clause: stands outside the clause structure; flags the note that follows
entries.pattern: N.B.: [clause]. · N.B. — [clause]. · Nota bene: [clause].
entries.punctuation: Written N.B. with a period after each letter, and followed by a colon, a dash, or nothing at all — but not by a comma, which is where it differs from i.e. and e.g. It normally opens its own sentence or parenthetical note.
entries.meaning: Latin note well, an imperative addressed to the reader. It is included here because it travels with i.e., e.g., and viz. and is punctuated by contrast with them, but it is worth being clear that it connects nothing: it is a flag on a note, not a link between clauses. Modern American writing increasingly just writes Note: instead.
examples: N.B.: The gallery is closed on Mondays and all federal holidays.
N.B. — all measurements in this table are given in millimeters.
Payment is due on the first of the month. N.B.: late fees apply after the fifth.
Nota bene: the second edition renumbers every chapter after the fourth.
N.B. The deposit becomes nonrefundable once the work begins.

entries.type: reader-directive cross-reference marker — not a conjunction
entries.clause: stands outside the clause; sends the reader to an entry elsewhere in the same work
entries.pattern: [term] (q.v.). · [term], q.v. · [two terms] (qq.v.).
entries.punctuation: Written q.v. with a period after each letter, normally inside parentheses immediately after the term it points at, and not followed by a comma. The plural, for two or more cross-references at once, is qq.v.
variants: cf. (a different instruction — compare, not consult)
entries.meaning: Latin quod vide, "which see" — an instruction to go and look up the term just named somewhere else in the same book. Its home is the reference work: encyclopedias, dictionaries, and legal treatises use it to mark a term that has an entry of its own. Do not confuse it with confer, which tells you to compare a source that differs; q.v. says the work itself covers the term elsewhere. Modern American editing largely replaces it with see and a page number, or with a link.
examples: The doctrine descends from the old writ of assumpsit (q.v.).
Compare the treatment of consideration (q.v.) in the chapter on contract formation.
The style was borrowed from the Aesthetic Movement (q.v.) a generation earlier.
On this point the reader should consult the entries for estoppel and laches (qq.v.).
The bird is closely related to the marsh harrier, q.v.

entries.clause: appositional phrase naming exactly what the preceding noun refers to
entries.pattern: [noun phrase], to wit, [specification]. · [clause], to wit: [list].
entries.punctuation: Commas on both sides — one item, to wit, the deed — or a comma before and a colon after when a list follows. Leaving off the second comma is a common error.
entries.meaning: The English calque of videlicet, from the old verb wit, meaning to know. Its home is the criminal charging document, where the offense is named in general terms and then pinned down precisely: one count of forgery, to wit, signing the endorsement on a check payable to another. Outside law it sounds theatrically stiff, which is exactly why writers reach for it to get a laugh.
examples: The defendant is charged with one count of forgery, to wit, signing the endorsement on a check made payable to another.
Two documents were produced, to wit: the lease and the addendum.
He was found in possession of the stolen property, to wit, a gold pocket watch.
Only one person had the combination, to wit, the branch manager.
The statute names three exceptions, to wit, fraud, duress, and mutual mistake.

entries.clause: appositional phrase introducing a complete specification or list
entries.pattern: [noun phrase], viz., [full list]. · [clause], viz. [specification].
entries.punctuation: Written viz. with a single period, and normally followed by a comma in American style. Read aloud as "namely," not as the Latin.
entries.meaning: Latin namely, contracted in medieval manuscripts to viz. — the z is really a scribal shorthand mark rather than a letter, which is why the pronunciation has nothing to do with it. It introduces the complete enumeration of what was just named in general terms, and that is what separates it from exempli gratia, which gives only a sample, and from inter alia, which says outright that the list is partial. Its rarer cousin scilicet (sc.) does a slightly different job: it supplies a word the text has left out, as in the poem's "she" (sc. the moon).
examples: Three species were recorded that night, viz., the barn owl, the screech owl, and the great horned owl.
Only one remedy is available to the plaintiff, viz., specific performance.
The manuscript names its sources, viz. Bede, Gildas, and Nennius.
He held two offices simultaneously, viz., treasurer and clerk.
The tax applies to a single class of property, viz., unimproved land.
